li.a: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: Hawn's Mill Massacre (Church History topic)
Alexander L. Baugh, "The Haun's Mill Massacre and the Extermination Order of Missouri Governor Lilburn W. Boggs," Mormon Historical Studies 10, no. 1 (2009)
Deseret News: Emily W. Jensen, "Setting the record straight on the 'Hawn's' Mill Massacre" (30 May 2010)
Missouri State Archives: Finding Aid 5.1, Mormon War Papers, 1837-1841 (letter of Daniel Ashby to General John B. Clark, 28 November 1838)

content.p: On the afternoon of 30 October 1838, a company of Missouri militiamen marched on a small Latter-day Saint settlement on Shoal Creek in eastern Caldwell County and opened fire. Seventeen Latter-day Saints were killed. The number of wounded is given as between twelve and fifteen, depending on who counts. The place was a mill and a cluster of families known as Hawn's Mill or Haun's Mill, and the killings there became known to Latter-day Saints as the Haun's Mill massacre. Alexander L. Baugh of Brigham Young University calls it the most tragic event in the church's history in terms of loss of life and injury inflicted by anti-Mormon forces. The attack took place three days after the state's governor had ordered the Latter-day Saints out of Missouri, and whether that order caused it remains uncertain, according to the accounts consulted.

Jacob Hawn, also written Haun, was one of the first settlers on Shoal Creek in northwestern Missouri and built a mill, and the place came to carry his name. The Church's history essay on the massacre describes the settlement as about a day's walk from Far West, the main Latter-day Saint gathering place in Caldwell County. Hawn himself never joined the church, though he got along well with the Saints who moved in near his mill in the late 1830s. Lightplanet's historical entry puts the number of families at the mill at thirty to forty when the attack came.

Deseret News reported in 2010 that Baugh had concluded the spelling should be Hawn. In family sources, Baugh found, the name is almost always written Hawn, and even grave markers use the w. State histories, county atlases and most later writing used Haun, and Baugh told the audience at a Mormon History Association conference in Independence that the older spelling had become so fixed on maps that it would be hard to change. Baugh also argued that the Hawns had reached Caldwell County before the Latter-day Saints and were never members of the church, a point that many earlier writers had got wrong. Baugh said it will take more research to learn whether Hawn's non-member status had repercussions for his perceived role in the massacre and aftermath.

The settlement sat in a county that had been filling with Latter-day Saint migrants since 1836. Joseph Smith had counseled Saints in places such as Hawn's Mill to move to Far West, and the Church's history essay notes that he later asked whether the killings might have been avoided if they had followed that advice. The essay's own answer is that it is hard to say. Some of the newcomers from Ohio had already been pressed by mobs on the road and had lost their weapons to them, and the essay says there may not have been a safe opportunity to reach Far West.
content.h2: The order and the months before
content.p: Through August, September and October 1838 the dispute between the Latter-day Saints and their Missouri neighbours grew into open fighting. On 27 October Governor Lilburn W. Boggs issued what became known as the Extermination Order, which told the Latter-day Saints to leave the state or be exterminated. Lightplanet's entry describes rumours that the Mormons planned to take Missouri land, and a fear that the population at Hawn's Mill would spread into non-Mormon Livingston County.

The timing has been argued over ever since. The Church's history essay says many have assumed that the order led to the massacre, and that some evidence suggests the attackers were not aware of it. It calls the massacre an act of vigilante violence, perhaps in revenge for Latter-day Saint raids in Daviess County. Lightplanet's entry says it is uncertain whether the order was a catalyst, but that both the Latter-day Saints and the Missourians believed their rights had been violated. Baugh's abstract calls the attackers an extralegal force of "county regulators."

Lightplanet's entry says that 200 to 250 militiamen from Livingston, Daviess and Carroll counties, acting under Colonel Thomas Jennings, arrived in the late afternoon. Baugh puts the force at more than two hundred men under Jennings of Livingston County. Lightplanet says the residents were surprised, because they assumed that an earlier truce still held. The church leader David Evans called for quarter, and the call was ignored. The women and children ran south across a stream and into the woods. The men and boys went into the blacksmith's shop, which offered little protection because the attackers could fire through the widely spaced logs of its walls.

The Church's history essay says the attackers shot repeatedly through the gaps, killing those inside and some who tried to surrender. It also says that several young boys who had hidden under the bellows were dragged out and shot. Lightplanet gives the names of individual victims, including a 78-year-old man who had surrendered his musket and was then shot and mutilated, and a ten-year-old boy found under the bellows. Amanda Barnes Smith wrote one of the best-known personal accounts of the day. Her husband and ten-year-old son were killed at the mill, where the family had stopped while moving from Ohio. The Church's essay says she prayed for guidance and received personal revelation while treating her seriously wounded seven-year-old son.

Baugh's abstract describes the victims as a non-threatening community that was almost entirely defenseless. Lightplanet says the attack was unprovoked, carried out during a time of truce, without any specific authority, by a far larger force, and with unusual brutality. Those are the words of the authors of those works, not findings of a court. Lightplanet says the 1838-39 Missouri judicial proceedings largely ignored the killings.
content.h2: The dead and the day after
content.p: The dead were thrown into an unfinished well near the mill and lightly covered with dirt and straw. Lightplanet says that a few Missourians came back the next day, took plunder and warned the Saints who remained to leave Missouri. The wounded were cared for by women while the men stayed hidden through the night.

The Church's essay gives the figure of seventeen killed and twelve to fifteen wounded. Lightplanet's entry counts seventeen Latter-day Saints and one friendly non-Mormon killed, with thirteen wounded, including a woman and a seven-year-old boy. Baugh puts the wounded at fourteen. Those differences are small. The figure for the attackers is less clear, because the two accounts give different numbers of militiamen wounded.

A letter written on 28 November 1838 by Daniel Ashby, a Missouri state senator, to General John B. Clark, who commanded the 1st Division of the Missouri militia, gives a very different picture. Ashby had been stationed in a reserve line and did not see how the firing began. He wrote that he had been told the Latter-day Saints fired first. He recalled a call for quarter from the militia's own side, after which a volley came from the creek, and said that the fight continued until no Mormon was left in sight except the wounded. Ashby also wrote that those who counted the dead found thirty-one Mormons killed, and that seven militiamen had been wounded. Lightplanet says that three militiamen were wounded and none killed. The state archive keeps Ashby's letter among its Mormon War papers, but the two figures differ, and this account gives no basis for choosing between them.

Lightplanet's entry says the 1838-39 judicial proceedings that investigated the Mormon War largely ignored the events at Haun's Mill, while Latter-day Saints wrote numerous and bitter accounts of the killings. Lightplanet says the attack became embedded in Latter-day Saint memory as an epitome of the cruel persecutions the Saints endured in Missouri.

Baugh said in 2010 that he had identified all of the Mormon victims, documented the Mormon defenders, and documented more than fifty of the Missouri vigilantes. The pages consulted report no charge or conviction arising from the killings.

Baugh's 2009 article in Mormon Historical Studies is written as a study of the massacre and the extermination order together. Taken together, the accounts agree on the core of what happened at Hawn's Mill: a surprise attack, seventeen dead, a well used as a grave, and proceedings that largely ignored the killings. They disagree on the number of wounded, the losses on the other side, the name of the mill's founder and whether the governor's order helped bring the attack about.
